ch.nm: Che Guevara: Living for Something Bigger I first heard about Che Guevara in seventh grade, when I was about thirteen. At that age most of us look for someone to admire, and he was the first person who made me think a life could be about more than yourself. What struck me was that he fought for people, not for personal gain. He gave up comfort and a stable career and chose sacrifice because he believed in something larger than his own interests. I know he is a complicated and debated figure, and I don't take him as a flawless hero. What stayed with me is the principle: do work that serves others, and be willing to pay a price for your convictions. That idea still shapes how I work today. I design for the people who will use the product, not for my own ego. Mike Tyson: The Mindset of a Fighter I'm a huge fan of Mike Tyson's boxing, but it's his mindset I respect most. He fought with ferocity and total commitment, and he also showed how hard the climb is, with success, collapse, and rebuilding. He taught me that discipline is what carries you when motivation disappears, and that you can fall hard and still rise. Fear is natural, and the answer is to walk toward it with preparation and nerve. Yukio Mishima: Discipline, Craft, and Beauty Mishima is my inspiration for writing, design, and style. I'm drawn to his obsession with form, with the idea that body and mind, art and discipline, should be shaped with the same seriousness. He turned himself from a frail young writer into a disciplined, physically trained man, and he held his craft to an uncompromising standard. In works like Confessions of a Mask and Sun and Steel, he explores identity, the body, and beauty with sharp precision. That sensibility runs through my design: clean lines, deliberate choices, nothing decorative without purpose. I take his devotion to craft, not his politics or his tragic end. From him I learned that style is not decoration. It is discipline made visible. Bruce Lee: Be Water I loved Bruce Lee's movies before I understood his philosophy. Later I realized his real genius was in refusing to be trapped by any single style. His idea of freestyle, absorbing what is useful, discarding what is not, and adding what is uniquely yours, is my approach to everything. As a hybrid athlete, I don't limit myself to one discipline. In design, I don't lock myself into one trend or method. I adapt to the problem in front of me. Rigid things break, and flowing things survive. Mike Mentzer: Intensity and Intelligence in Training Mike Mentzer is my guide in bodybuilding. His philosophy of high-intensity training taught me that growth does not come from endless volume or mindless repetition. It comes from effort that is hard, purposeful, and followed by proper recovery. Train with full intensity, think about what you do, and respect rest. This is the foundation of my life as a hybrid athlete. I love lifting, conditioning, and pushing my limits, and Mentzer gave my training a rational structure. The lesson reaches beyond the gym: quality of effort matters more than quantity of hours. Stoicism: The Mind That Holds It All Together If the others are my inspirations, Stoicism is the framework that connects them. It teaches me to separate what I control from what I don't. I can control my effort, my choices, and my response. I can't control outcomes, other people's opinions, or luck. That clarity keeps me steady when a client is difficult, a lift fails, or a plan collapses. Obstacles are not interruptions to the path. They are the path. I try to meet each one with calm and discipline. Bringing It Together Che gave me purpose, Tyson resilience, Mishima craft, Bruce Lee adaptability, Mentzer intensity with intelligence, and Stoicism the calm to carry all of it. I am a designer, an athlete, and a student of life, and I try to bring the same principles to every pixel I design and every rep I lift: serve something bigger than yourself, work with intensity, master your craft, stay flexible, and keep your mind steady. That is my ideology, and it is also how I design.
